h1: Load Bearing Wall Removal in Perth: Beam Design and Engineering
heroSub: Planning an open-plan kitchen? Send photos and plans, and an independent structural engineer will quote to check the wall and design the beam, posts and footings that a registered builder then installs.
introHtml:
Load bearing wall removal in Perth nearly always starts with a brick house. WA is the only state where more than half of detached houses are brick, at 68 per cent, and in a double-brick home the inner leaf of the external walls and some internal walls usually carry the ceiling, the roof or an upper floor. So the wall between your kitchen and lounge may well be holding something up. Find out before anyone picks up a hammer.

Kings Park Structural Co is advertising, not an engineering firm. We pass your enquiry to the independent structural engineering firm that advertises here, and it quotes you and contracts with you directly. The engineer who takes your job works out what the wall carries, sizes the beam and its supports, and provides the drawing and certificate your building surveyor needs. A registered builder does the building work.

features.title: Load path check
features.desc: The engineer traces what sits on the wall (roof framing, ceiling, an upper floor or another wall) and where that load has to go once the wall is gone.

features.title: Steel or LVL beam sizing
features.desc: The beam is sized for your span and your loads, with bearing lengths and connections specified so the builder isn't guessing on site.

features.title: Posts, point loads and pad footings
features.desc: A beam dumps its load at each end. The design covers the posts or brick piers there and any pad footing needed underneath.

features.title: Temporary propping
features.desc: The roof and ceiling have to be held up while the wall comes out. Ask the engineer to cover propping in the documents so the builder works to a plan.

features.title: Drawing and certificate for the permit
features.desc: You get a beam specification or drawing and a signed certificate that your building surveyor can rely on when the permit application goes in.

features.title: Clear split of who does what
features.desc: The engineer assesses and designs. A registered builder removes the wall and installs the beam, and the permit comes from the council or a building surveyor.

sections.heading: How to tell if a wall is load bearing
sections.html:
There are clues you can check yourself, and they're worth knowing before you ring anyone. None of them is proof either way, and none of them tells you a wall is safe to remove.

  • It's double brick. In a full-masonry house some internal walls typically carry ceilings and roof, not just the external walls.
  • Something in the roof space lands on it: a strut, a prop or a beam sitting on or just above the wall.
  • There's a wall or a floor directly above it on a second storey.
  • Cornice cracks, sagging ceiling lines or sticking doors near the wall. These can point to movement, and that's a job for a structural inspection before any removal plan.

The rules take the guessing out of the permit question. Under WA's Building Regulations, renovation work is only exempt from a building permit if it doesn't remove or alter an element that helps support another element. A load-bearing wall is exactly that, so its removal needs a permit and engineering behind it.

sections.heading: What the engineer needs from you
sections.html:
A good quote comes from good information. Most engineers start with photos and whatever plans you have, then decide whether they need to see the house in person.

  • Photos of both faces of the wall, the ceiling line along it and the rooms either side.
  • Photos from the roof space above the wall, showing any struts, props or beams sitting on or near it.
  • The house plans if you have them. Your council may hold a copy of the original approved drawings.
  • Rough measurements: wall length, ceiling height, and how wide you want the opening.
  • What's above: single storey, an upper floor, or a tiled or Colorbond roof.

If you're also adding floor area, the job becomes an extension and the engineering grows with it; see extension engineering. Engineers cover Greater Perth, the Perth Hills and Peel, from Joondalup and Wanneroo down to Mandurah. Call (08) 5550 6237 now to get the photos in front of one.

sections.heading: What you get, and who builds it
sections.html:
The engineer's output is paperwork, not a new opening. Expect a beam specification or drawing showing the beam size and grade, the posts or piers, any pad footings and the fixings, plus a signed certificate. Under the Building Act, a certified permit application must include each technical certificate the building surveyor relied on, and the engineer's certificate can be one of them.

You then choose a permit route. A certified application (BA1) goes in with a certificate of design compliance from a registered private building surveyor, and the permit authority has 10 business days to decide. An uncertified application (BA2) lets the council's own surveyors assess it, with 25 business days to decide. Both clocks stop if the council asks for more information.

A registered builder does the demolition, propping and beam installation. Residential building work over $20,000 must be covered by home indemnity insurance, and that's the builder's job to arrange. From 1 July 2027, structural engineering in WA must be done by a registered building engineer, and you can check anyone's registration on the DEMIRS Building Engineer Register.

sections.heading: What load bearing wall removal costs in Perth
sections.html:
No Perth engineering firm publishes a fixed fee for beam design. Engineers quote each job, and the price depends on the house, the span, what sits on the wall and what the council wants to see. Send photos and you'll get a written quote from the engineer before any work starts.

The government charges are published, and they're calculated on the estimated value of the work including GST:

  • Certified building permit: 0.19% of the value, minimum $121.00.
  • Uncertified building permit: 0.32% of the value, minimum $121.00.
  • Building Services Levy: $61.65 if the work is $45,000 or less, or 0.137% above that.
  • Construction Training Fund levy: 0.2%, but only where the work is worth more than $100,000.

On a $30,000 kitchen-and-wall job, 0.19% comes to $57, so the $121.00 minimum applies, plus the $61.65 levy. The builder's price for the beam, propping and making good is separate. Our structural engineer cost guide covers the rest.

faq.q: Do I need a building permit to remove a load-bearing wall in Perth?
faq.a: Yes. WA's Building Regulations only exempt renovation work that doesn't remove or alter an element supporting another element, and a load-bearing wall does exactly that. A certified permit costs 0.19% of the value of the work including GST, and an uncertified one 0.32%, both with a $121.00 minimum. Whether a permit is granted is up to the permit authority.

faq.q: How much does a structural engineer charge for beam design in Perth?
faq.a: No Perth engineering firm publishes a set fee, so the engineer quotes after seeing photos, plans or the site. What you can budget for exactly is the government side: at least $121.00 for the permit and $61.65 for the Building Services Levy on work of $45,000 or less. The builder's price for the beam and installation comes on top.

faq.q: How long does the permit take?
faq.a: The permit authority has 10 business days to decide a certified application and 25 business days for an uncertified one. The clock stops if the council asks for more information, so a complete engineer's drawing and certificate helps. The engineer gives you their own turnaround when they quote.

faq.q: Can an engineer tell from photos whether my wall is load bearing?
faq.a: Photos of the wall, the roof space above it and any plans are the usual starting point, and they let the engineer quote. Whether that's enough, or a site visit is needed, is the engineer's call. With 68 per cent of WA detached houses built of brick, don't touch a wall on a hunch or on a builder's glance.

faq.q: Who actually removes the wall and puts the beam in?
faq.a: A registered builder, working to the engineer's design. Engineers assess and design; they don't do building work. Residential work over $20,000 must be covered by the builder's home indemnity insurance, and from 1 July 2027 the engineering itself must be done by a registered building engineer, with fines of up to $25,000 for unregistered work.
